transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Um… I guess I’m here because my eating has gotten kind of out of control. Especially at night. I’ll be grading papers, and I start with just some leftovers, and then somehow I’ve gone through cereal, crackers, peanut butter… even snacks I packed for my classroom, which is embarrassing because then the next day I’m pretending I just “forgot” them. It’s like the amount of food scares me afterward.
Do you feel guilty after these late-night eating episodes?

I… I don’t really know how to answer that cleanly. I know I feel awful afterward, but “guilty” is kind of a loaded word, I guess. Like, sometimes I’m more just sitting there looking at the wrappers and bowls and thinking, how did that even happen?

And then I start worrying about stupid practical things, like whether I’ll have enough snacks left for the kids’ reward bin, or if I need to stop at the store before school, and then I’m mad at myself for making the morning harder. So… maybe guilt? I’m not sure.
Do you feel like you're unable to stop eating once you start during these late-night episodes?

Yeah. I mean… yes, that’s probably the part that scares me most. Once I start, it’s like the reasonable teacher part of me is standing off to the side going, Joan, stop, you have school tomorrow, this is enough. And then my hands just keep opening things anyway.

It’s weird because in my classroom I’m so organized—like, I can get twenty-eight kids lined up after recess, mostly, depending on the day—and at home I can’t even seem to stop myself from opening another box or jar. I’ll keep eating until I’m painfully full, like physically uncomfortable, and I still feel like I wasn’t really in charge of it.
Do you feel like you're in control of what you're eating during these episodes?

No, not really. I mean, I know technically I’m the one doing it, but it doesn’t feel like I’m deciding each thing.

It’s like this… the sensible teacher part of me is watching from somewhere outside my body, saying, Joan, stop, this is enough, you’re going to feel awful. And then my hands just keep opening something else, or putting more food in my mouth anyway. It’s almost embarrassing to say, because I can manage a classroom full of kids better than I can manage myself in my own kitchen.

By the time I kind of come back to myself, I’m usually painfully full. So… no, I don’t feel in control during it.
Is it the amount of food that you're eating during these episodes that makes you feel like you've lost control?

Yeah… I think the amount is a big part of it. It’s not like I’m just having an extra bowl of cereal or something normal like that.

I’ll start with, I don’t know, leftovers while I’m grading papers, and then somehow it turns into cereal, crackers, peanut butter on a spoon, and then I’m digging into the snacks I packed for my classroom. Which is ridiculous, because those are supposed to be for the kids, like for little rewards or if someone forgot snack, and then I’m standing there thinking about whether I need to replace them before school.

So yes… the amount scares me. It feels like way more than I meant to eat, way more than makes sense.
Do you usually feel stressed, anxious, or upset right before these late-night eating episodes?

I’m not totally sure. I mean, sometimes I’ve had a long day, but honestly most school days are long days, you know? Especially with the kids getting restless or someone crying because their glue stick “looked at them funny”—which sounds silly, but by 3 p.m. it really does feel like a lot.

But right before it happens… I don’t know if I’d say I always notice feeling stressed or anxious. Sometimes I’m just home and tired, doing normal evening things, and then it sort of… happens. I haven’t been great at paying attention to what I’m feeling right before.
Do you think you're eating at night because you're feeling emotional, like upset or stressed, or is it more just because you're hungry or bored?

I don’t really know. I wish I had a neat answer, like “yes, it’s stress” or “no, I’m just hungry,” but I honestly haven’t figured that out.

Sometimes I think maybe I’m tired more than anything. After school my brain feels like it’s been making tiny decisions all day—who needs help, who’s about to throw a pencil, whose parent emailed—and then at night I’m just… sort of blank. But I don’t always feel upset in a clear way. And I wouldn’t say I’m sitting there thinking, oh, I’m bored, let me eat.

It just sort of starts, and then I’m already in it before I’ve labeled what I was feeling. So… maybe emotions are part of it, but I’m not sure I notice them at the time.
Do you feel like you're eating really quickly during these late-night episodes?

I’m not sure… I haven’t really clocked the speed of it, if that makes sense.

Like, I know it feels kind of automatic, but whether I’m eating fast-fast or just not paying attention, I don’t know. Sometimes I’ll be standing in the kitchen, and then I’m thinking about how I need to laminate something for my class or whether I answered a parent email, and then suddenly more food is gone than I expected.

So… maybe? But I don’t think I’ve paid enough attention to say for sure.
Do you usually eat a large amount of food in a very short period of time during these episodes?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, that’s kind of why I finally came in, because it feels like an amount that scares me afterward.

Like I’ll start with something normal, like leftovers while I’m grading papers, and then somehow I’ve also had cereal, crackers, peanut butter, and then I’m digging into the snacks I bought for my classroom. Which is embarrassing because those are supposed to be for the kids, or for emergencies, and then I’m mentally adding “buy more Goldfish” to my list like that’s the main problem.

So… yes, I think it is a lot in not a lot of time. It doesn’t feel normal when I look back at it.
Do you feel like these late-night eating episodes are affecting your daily life or causing you significant distress?

Yeah… it is. I mean, I keep trying to act like it’s just a night problem, like it happens and then the next day I’ll reset, but it kind of takes over everything around it.

My evenings end up being about… trying to fix it, I guess. Or planning around it. And then weekends too, when I should be catching up on grading or seeing people or doing laundry—actually my laundry has been ridiculous lately, there are like three baskets just sitting there—but instead I’m thinking about what happened with food, or what I’m going to do to make up for it.

And at work I’m still functioning, like I show up and the kids get what they need, but I’m slower with grading and prep than I used to be. I feel like I’m spending so much energy trying to seem normal and put-together, because teachers are supposed to be, you know, calm and organized and have matching bins. And then with friends I’m kind of there but not really there. I’ll be listening, but part of me is still worrying about food or how I look or whether they can tell something’s off.

So yes. It’s distressing. More than I want to admit, probably.
Do you feel like you're unable to stop yourself from continuing to eat once you've started during these episodes?

Yeah… yes. That’s probably the scariest part.

It’s like once I start, there’s this reasonable teacher part of me—like the part that can manage twenty-eight kids arguing over scissors and still remember who needs their reading folder signed—that part is kind of standing off to the side going, “Joan, stop. You don’t need more. Put it away.” But my hands just keep doing it. Opening things, getting another spoon, going back to the cupboard, putting food in my mouth.

And I’ll think, okay, after this bite I’m done, or after this one thing I’ll stop, and then I just… don’t. I keep going until I’m so full it hurts, and then I’m sitting there like, how did I let it get there again?
Do you feel ashamed of yourself after these late-night eating episodes?

I… I don’t know if I’d call it shame exactly. Maybe? I’m not sure.

I definitely don’t feel good afterward. I’ll sort of sit there and think, “What was that?” and then I get really quiet with myself, if that makes sense. Like I don’t want to look too closely at it.

But “ashamed” feels like a big word. I mean, I tell my students all the time that mistakes aren’t moral failures, and then of course I don’t apply that to myself, because apparently I’m only wise with seven-year-olds holding broken crayons. So… maybe there’s some of that. I just don’t know how to separate shame from embarrassment or regret or just feeling really uncomfortable with myself afterward.
Do you feel guilty after these episodes, looking back on what happened?

I’m not totally sure. I mean… maybe? It’s hard for me to tell the difference between guilt and just this awful “ugh, why did I do that” feeling.

Sometimes I’ll look around afterward and it’s like when my classroom is a mess after an art project—glue sticks without caps, paper scraps everywhere, someone somehow got marker on the chair—and I know I have to clean it up, but it’s also this sinking feeling of, “How did it get this out of hand?” Except with this, it’s me, so it feels more personal.

But guilty… I don’t know. I don’t always have a clear thought like “I did something wrong.” It’s more like I want to move on really fast and not think about it too much.
How often do these late-night eating episodes happen?

Lately… pretty often, I guess. I’m trying to think of it like a calendar, because otherwise it all blurs together with school weeks and lesson planning and whether I remembered to buy more glue sticks—sorry.

For the past few months, I’d say there’s rarely been a week where it doesn’t happen at least one night. Sometimes it feels like I’ll have one of those nights where I eat way more than I meant to, and then the next day I sort of… try to balance it out. Like I won’t really eat at school, or I’ll tell myself I’m too busy, which is easy because lunch duty is chaos anyway. Or I’ll push myself to do a really long walk or extra yoga after work.

So… at least weekly, most weeks. Maybe that’s the simplest answer.
Do you ever find that you don't remember eating some of the food during these episodes?

I’m not sure. I don’t think I black out or anything like that. It’s more like… I know I was in the kitchen, I know I was eating, but afterward it can feel kind of blurry in the way a stressful school day blurs together.

Like, I’ll remember pieces—opening something, standing at the counter, maybe putting a wrapper in the trash—but not in a neat order. It’s not like when a student asks me where their lunchbox is and I genuinely have no idea, because there are twenty-seven tiny emergencies happening at once. This is more… I was there, I just wasn’t paying attention to myself very well.

So I guess I haven’t really noticed “not remembering eating” exactly. More like not wanting to think about it afterward.
Do you ever try to make up for what you've eaten during these episodes by doing something to compensate, like exercising or restricting your food intake the next day?

Yeah… I do. I mean, I don’t think of it as “compensating” in the moment exactly, but that’s basically what it is.

After one of those nights, I’ll wake up and decide I’m not allowed to eat breakfast, and then at school I’ll skip lunch too. It’s easy to make excuses because there’s always something—copies jammed in the machine, someone crying because their pencil broke, a parent email I forgot to answer… so I can tell myself I’m just too busy.

And then later I’ll go out on the trail for way too long, or do extra yoga even if I’m already shaky and exhausted. Like I know my body is saying, “please stop,” but my head is saying I have to make up for it somehow.
Do you ever try to make up for what you've eaten during these episodes by purging or using laxatives?

I… I don’t really know how to answer that cleanly. Purging, like… making myself throw up? I’m not sure I want to get into the details wrong and then have it sound more definite than it is.

I’ve definitely done the “I’ll fix it tomorrow” thing, like we were saying, where I make rules for myself and then the whole next day at school becomes this weird math problem in my head. Which is ridiculous because I’m literally teaching kids fractions and then I’m doing my own secret, awful version of it in the background.

Laxatives… I don’t know. I mean, I know what you mean, but I haven’t really thought of it that way, if that makes sense. I guess I’m not sure.
Have you ever made yourself throw up after one of these late-night eating episodes?

I… I don’t know. I’m sorry, that’s probably not a helpful answer.

I keep getting stuck on the wording, like “made myself” sounds so clear and intentional, and I don’t know if I can say it that way. After those nights I’m usually so ashamed that I sort of just want the whole thing to disappear, if that makes sense.

Sorry, I’m going off. It’s like when a kid in my class asks me if I’m mad and I’m trying to answer without making them feel worse, and then suddenly I’m explaining my entire morning. I’m not trying to avoid your question. I just… I’m not sure how to answer it simply.
Have you ever made yourself throw up after eating?

I’m… not sure I can say yes to that. I know that sounds evasive, and I hate that, because I’m usually the person telling my students, “Use your words, be specific,” and then here I am being completely vague.

After eating, especially if I feel really panicky about it, I’ll feel like I need to do something, or I’ll stand in the bathroom and just sort of spiral. But “made myself throw up” feels like such a specific thing, and I don’t know if that’s exactly what happened or if I’m just… remembering the shame more than the details.

So I guess the honest answer is I don’t really know how to answer that clearly.
Have you ever intentionally made yourself vomit after eating?

I’m still getting caught on the word intentionally. Like… I know that probably sounds like I’m splitting hairs, but in my head there’s a difference between feeling so upset and sick and standing there thinking, “I can’t have done that,” versus calmly deciding to do something.

I don’t know how to make that into a clean yes-or-no answer. I’m sorry. I think I’m worried if I say it the wrong way, it becomes this label or this thing that sounds more clear than it feels. It’s kind of like when I write report card comments and I’m trying to be accurate but not unfair, and I rewrite one sentence ten times because one word changes the whole meaning.

So… I don’t know. I can tell you I’ve felt really panicked after eating and like I needed to undo it somehow, but I’m not sure I can clearly say, “yes, I intentionally made myself vomit.”

Sometimes it feels like I’ll have one of those nights where I eat way more than I meant to, and then the next day I sort of… try to balance it out. Like I won’t really eat at school, or I’ll tell myself I’m too busy, which is easy because lunch duty is chaos anyway. Or I’ll push myself to do a really long walk or extra yoga after work.

So… at least weekly, most weeks. Maybe that’s the simplest answer.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's eating episodes are accompanied by a lack of recall for what they ate
doctor.question: Do you ever find that you don't remember eating some of the food during these episodes?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about not remembering eating some of the food during episodes, which relates to memory gaps or dissociation; this is not covered by the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure. I don’t think I black out or anything like that. It’s more like… I know I was in the kitchen, I know I was eating, but afterward it can feel kind of blurry in the way a stressful school day blurs together.

Like, I’ll remember pieces—opening something, standing at the counter, maybe putting a wrapper in the trash—but not in a neat order. It’s not like when a student asks me where their lunchbox is and I genuinely have no idea, because there are twenty-seven tiny emergencies happening at once. This is more… I was there, I just wasn’t paying attention to myself very well.

So I guess I haven’t really noticed “not remembering eating” exactly. More like not wanting to think about it afterward.

doctor.intent: determine presence of compensatory behaviors
doctor.question: Do you ever try to make up for what you've eaten during these episodes by doing something to compensate, like exercising or restricting your food intake the next day?

target_item.name: Compensatory_Behavior_NonPurging
target_item.manifestation: After one of those nights, I’ll tell myself I’m not allowed to eat breakfast or lunch at school, and then I’ll stay out on the trail for hours or do extra yoga even when I’m shaky and exhausted.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking whether I compensate after eating episodes by restricting food intake or exercising, which matches non-purging compensatory behavior.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I do. I mean, I don’t think of it as “compensating” in the moment exactly, but that’s basically what it is.

After one of those nights, I’ll wake up and decide I’m not allowed to eat breakfast, and then at school I’ll skip lunch too. It’s easy to make excuses because there’s always something—copies jammed in the machine, someone crying because their pencil broke, a parent email I forgot to answer… so I can tell myself I’m just too busy.

And then later I’ll go out on the trail for way too long, or do extra yoga even if I’m already shaky and exhausted. Like I know my body is saying, “please stop,” but my head is saying I have to make up for it somehow.

doctor.intent: determine if patient uses compensatory behaviors to counteract the binge eating
doctor.question: Do you ever try to make up for what you've eaten during these episodes by purging or using laxatives?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about purging or laxative use, but the provided symptom profile only includes non-purging compensatory behaviors such as restriction, excessive exercise, and yoga.

patient.answer:
I… I don’t really know how to answer that cleanly. Purging, like… making myself throw up? I’m not sure I want to get into the details wrong and then have it sound more definite than it is.

I’ve definitely done the “I’ll fix it tomorrow” thing, like we were saying, where I make rules for myself and then the whole next day at school becomes this weird math problem in my head. Which is ridiculous because I’m literally teaching kids fractions and then I’m doing my own secret, awful version of it in the background.

Laxatives… I don’t know. I mean, I know what you mean, but I haven’t really thought of it that way, if that makes sense. I guess I’m not sure.

doctor.intent: determine if patient uses purging as a means of compensation
doctor.question: Have you ever made yourself throw up after one of these late-night eating episodes?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about self-induced vomiting/purging after eating episodes, but the provided symptom profile only includes non-purging compensatory behaviors such as restriction and excessive exercise, not purging.

patient.answer:
I… I don’t know. I’m sorry, that’s probably not a helpful answer.

I keep getting stuck on the wording, like “made myself” sounds so clear and intentional, and I don’t know if I can say it that way. After those nights I’m usually so ashamed that I sort of just want the whole thing to disappear, if that makes sense.

Sorry, I’m going off. It’s like when a kid in my class asks me if I’m mad and I’m trying to answer without making them feel worse, and then suddenly I’m explaining my entire morning. I’m not trying to avoid your question. I just… I’m not sure how to answer it simply.

doctor.intent: determine if patient engages in purging behavior
doctor.question: Have you ever made yourself throw up after eating?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about self-induced vomiting/purging after eating, but the provided symptom profile only covers non-purging compensatory behaviors and does not include a purging symptom item.

patient.answer:
I’m… not sure I can say yes to that. I know that sounds evasive, and I hate that, because I’m usually the person telling my students, “Use your words, be specific,” and then here I am being completely vague.

After eating, especially if I feel really panicky about it, I’ll feel like I need to do something, or I’ll stand in the bathroom and just sort of spiral. But “made myself throw up” feels like such a specific thing, and I don’t know if that’s exactly what happened or if I’m just… remembering the shame more than the details.

So I guess the honest answer is I don’t really know how to answer that clearly.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has engaged in purging behavior
doctor.question: Have you ever intentionally made yourself vomit after eating?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about intentional vomiting/purging after eating, but the provided symptom profile only includes non-purging compensatory behaviors and does not cover self-induced vomiting.

patient.answer:
I’m still getting caught on the word intentionally. Like… I know that probably sounds like I’m splitting hairs, but in my head there’s a difference between feeling so upset and sick and standing there thinking, “I can’t have done that,” versus calmly deciding to do something.

I don’t know how to make that into a clean yes-or-no answer. I’m sorry. I think I’m worried if I say it the wrong way, it becomes this label or this thing that sounds more clear than it feels. It’s kind of like when I write report card comments and I’m trying to be accurate but not unfair, and I rewrite one sentence ten times because one word changes the whole meaning.

So… I don’t know. I can tell you I’ve felt really panicked after eating and like I needed to undo it somehow, but I’m not sure I can clearly say, “yes, I intentionally made myself vomit.”
